title: Money talks
goals: Deduce what happened in the past with must have / can't have / might have + past participle, grading the certainty.
Use the continuous form (must have been working) and distinguish present deduction (must be) from past deduction.
Differentiate deduction from reproach or regret: should have, shouldn't have, needn't have, could have.
Speculate with nuance and register: presumably, be bound to, seem to have, for all we know.
Talk about personal finance, ethical consumption and money idioms (break the bank, make ends meet).
Debate dilemmas and speculate about causes with a polite tone and balanced arguments.

learn.title: Deduction about the past: must / can't / might + have + past participle
learn.html:
When something has already happened but you are not sure and you reason from clues, you use a modal verb + have + past participle. The modal shows how certain you are; the verb only says what you think happened. Think of a scale:

CertaintyStructureExample
~95% (yes)must have + past participleThe safe is open: someone must have known the code.
~95% (no)can't / couldn't have + past participleShe can't have seen the email; her account was locked.
Possiblemay / might / could have + past participleHe might have lost it on the train.
Possibly notmay not / might not have + past participleThey might not have received the invoice.

Watch out for Spanish: «debe de haber» and «tiene que haber» are both translated with must have; but the opposite of «debe de haber» is NOT mustn't have. To say «no puede haber» (certainty), English uses can't have or couldn't have. Mustn't expresses prohibition, not deduction.

Key difference: can't have and may not have are not equivalent: She can't have known = I am almost sure she did NOT know; She may not have known = perhaps she did not know (I do not rule out the opposite).

Continuous aspect and passive: for activities that were in progress: He must have been working all night (he looks exhausted). For the passive: The card might have been stolen. With could have, context decides between past possibility («podría haber pasado») and a missed opportunity («podría haberlo hecho»).

watch.wrong: She must had spent all her savings on that trip.
watch.right: She must have spent all her savings on that trip.
watch.why: After a modal comes have (base form), not had.

watch.wrong: He mustn't have known about the debt.
watch.right: He can't have known about the debt.
watch.why: To deny something with certainty use can't/couldn't have, not mustn't have.

watch.wrong: They can't have been knowing the risks.
watch.right: They can't have known the risks.
watch.why: Know is a stative verb: it is not used in the continuous.

watch.wrong: He should of checked the interest rate.
watch.right: He should have checked the interest rate.
watch.why: It sounds like 'of' because 've is pronounced like 'of', but the correct form is have.

learn.title: Present, past and continuous: contrast
learn.html:
The modal stays the same; what changes is the infinitive that follows it and therefore the time the deduction refers to.

TimeStructureExample
Present statemust / can't / might + beShe must be rich; look at that car.
Action in progress nowmust / might + be + V-ingThey must be having dinner; nobody answers.
Past (completed action)must / can't / might + have + past participleHe must have taken a loan.
Past in progressmust / might + have been + V-ingHe must have been saving for years.
Future / sure habitbe bound to / is likely to + infinitivePrices are bound to rise.

couldn't vs. can't: with have they are almost interchangeable in current English (She can't / couldn't have forgotten); couldn't sounds slightly more natural and less absolute in past narration. Could have (affirmative), by contrast, expresses only possibility: It could have been a fraud.

If there is direct evidence, you do not need to deduce: He spent a fortune (I know it) vs. He must have spent a fortune (I infer it). Using must when you know the fact sounds odd.

Register: in speech, must've, can't've, might've are contracted; in formal writing they are written in full.

watch.wrong: He must be left early; his desk is empty.
watch.right: He must have left early; his desk is empty.
watch.why: Past event: must have + past participle.

watch.wrong: She must be working all night; she looks exhausted.
watch.right: She must have been working all night; she looks exhausted.
watch.why: The work happened in the past: must have been + V-ing.

watch.wrong: The shop is closed. It must have been a holiday today.
watch.right: The shop is closed. It must be a holiday today.
watch.why: You are talking about the present: must be.

watch.wrong: I'm sure they have been won the lottery.
watch.right: I'm sure they must have won the lottery.
watch.why: To deduce you need the modal; won is the past participle.

learn.title: Modals of reproach and regret (not to be confused with deduction)
learn.html:
The same modal + have + past participle structure is also used to judge what happened, not to guess it. The context completely changes the meaning:

StructureMeaningExample
should / ought to have + past participleIt was the right or advisable thing to do and it was not done (reproach, regret)You should have read the small print.
shouldn't have + past participleSomething was done that should not have beenI shouldn't have lent him the money.
could have + past participleMissed opportunity: it was possible and was not doneWe could have saved more.
needn't have + past participleSomething was done that was NOT necessaryYou needn't have paid the whole bill (but you did).
didn't need to + baseIt was not necessary (and perhaps it was not done)You didn't need to pay (so maybe you didn't).

Politeness and register: You should have told me sounds like a direct reproach. Soften it: It might have been better to check first; Perhaps you could have mentioned it earlier. In formal contexts: It would have been preferable to….

How to tell deduction from reproach: ask yourself whether you are talking about what probably happened (must/can't/might) or what should have happened and did not (should/could/needn't). She must have saved a lot (conclusion) vs. She should have saved more (judgement).

watch.wrong: You mustn't have paid so much; it's far too expensive.
watch.right: You can't have paid so much; it's far too expensive.
watch.why: It is a negative deduction, not a prohibition.

watch.wrong: You needn't to have bought a present.
watch.right: You needn't have bought a present.
watch.why: Needn't is a modal: no to, followed by have + past participle.

watch.wrong: I should have went to the bank earlier.
watch.right: I should have gone to the bank earlier.
watch.why: Should have + past participle (gone), not simple past.

watch.wrong: She shouldn't to have said that.
watch.why: Shouldn't is a modal: no to, and it is followed by have + past participle.

learn.title: Other ways to speculate and qualify
learn.html:
At C1 level, must / might are not enough. To speculate with nuance and a varied register you have adverbs, perception verbs and impersonal structures. Ordered by degree of certainty:

DegreeResourcesExample
Very likelymust have, be bound to have, in all likelihood, presumablyPresumably he has already left; he's bound to have heard.
Likelybe likely to have, I'd imagine / I suspect (that), it seems / appears thatThey're likely to have overpaid; I suspect the fee was hidden.
Possiblemay / might / could have, quite possibly, conceivably, it's possible thatConceivably, the bank misread the form.
Unlikelybe unlikely to have, hardly / can't possibly have, it's highly improbable thatShe can't possibly have known.
No informationfor all we know, who knows whetherFor all we know, he gave it all away.

Seem / appear to have + past participle: He seems to have lost interest (≈ it appears that he has lost interest). The impersonal form is more academic: It appears that the funds were transferred twice. With is thought / said / believed to have + past participle one reports a general opinion (see the passive units).

To debate a dilemma: It could be argued that…; On the one hand… on the other…; That would explain why…; The most plausible explanation is that…

watch.wrong: She is probably have forgotten the password.
watch.right: She has probably forgotten the password.
watch.why: Probably + present perfect or modal; they do not combine.

watch.right: He's likely to have gone bankrupt.
watch.why: Be likely + to have + past participle.

watch.wrong: Maybe he might have lost the receipt.
watch.right: He might have lost the receipt.
watch.why: Maybe and might repeat the doubt: use only one.

watch.wrong: It seems that he have spent too much.
watch.right: It seems that he has spent too much.
watch.why: After it seems that, use a finite verb: has spent; or seem to have + past participle.

learn.title: Speculating and debating a dilemma
learn.html:
• That would explain why … — link a clue to a cause: That would explain why he stopped going out.
  • There has to be an explanation. / There must be a logical reason. — insist that there is a cause.
  • For all we know, … — remind yourself that information is missing.
  • It could be argued that … / One could say that … — introduce an argument with some distance.
  • On the one hand … on the other (hand) … — set out the sides of a dilemma.
  • I'd say it's a toss-up. — it's evenly balanced; you cannot tell.
  • If I were in her shoes, I'd … — put yourself in the other person's position.
  • Let's not jump to conclusions. — stop a hasty speculation.
  • Fair point. / Good point, but … — concede and qualify.

Tone: when speculating about other people, use might / may and seem to so as not to sound accusatory.

write.prompt: Write an essay of 250 to 350 words: «Should we judge people by how they spend their money?». Present both sides (ethical consumption, saving, spending), use at least three speculations about the past (must have / can't have / might have) and two modals of reproach or regret (should have / needn't have). Include financial vocabulary and two money idioms.
checklist: Between 250 and 350 words, with introduction, two sides of the debate and conclusion
3 or more deductions/speculations about the past with the correct structure
2 modals of reproach (should have / needn't have / shouldn't have)
Distinguish can't have from may not have
Vocabulary: afford, budget, debt, ethical consumption, frugal, accountable
2 idioms (break the bank, make ends meet…)
Debate expressions (It could be argued…, On the one hand…)
write.model:
It is tempting to judge people by the way they spend their money. A neighbour arrives in a new sports car, and we assume he must have received a promotion. A colleague turns up in the same worn coat every winter, and we think she must be frugal, or perhaps struggling. But how reliable are such judgements?

On the one hand, it could be argued that spending reveals values. Someone who buys only second-hand clothes or supports local producers is practising ethical consumption, and it seems fair to hold such people accountable when they preach sustainability while flying abroad every month. Similarly, those who run up large debts on luxuries might be seen as reckless; they should have kept a budget, and a family that can barely afford its rent surely needn't have bought the latest television.

On the other hand, appearances can be deeply misleading. The man with the sports car may have inherited it, or he may be leasing it at great sacrifice. He can't have received a promotion, since the firm froze salaries last year, yet he may not have paid for it himself either. Likewise, the woman in the worn coat might have been saving for her children's education, or she could simply have been making ends meet after losing a job. Nor does an expensive purchase necessarily break the bank; for some people, a single treat is a rare relief from months of caution.

Moreover, judgements about money ignore circumstance. Those who live on a tight income often have little choice, and criticising them is as unfair as praising the wealthy for choices that cost them nothing.

In conclusion, while spending can tell us something about priorities, it rarely tells the whole story. We should have been more careful before drawing conclusions from a stranger's wallet. It seems wiser to ask what people value than to count what they buy.

write.prompt: In 250 to 350 words, write a short news report about an invented financial mystery (for example, an employee who suddenly changes their lifestyle, or a huge anonymous donation). Put forward at least four hypotheses with different degrees of certainty and rule one out with can't have.
checklist: Between 250 and 350 words
4 hypotheses with different degrees of certainty (must / might / could / can't have)
At least one continuous modal (must have been + V-ing)
Other devices: presumably, for all we know, seem to have
Financial vocabulary
Journalistic style and well-connected paragraphs
No 'mustn't have' or 'should of'
write.model:
MYSTERY SURROUNDS ACCOUNTANT'S SUDDEN WEALTH

Residents of the small town of Alderbury are puzzled by the transformation of a local accountant who, within the space of three months, has swapped a ten-year-old hatchback for a luxury car, donated generously to the church roof appeal and booked a year-long trip abroad.

Henry Vaughn, 42, has worked at the town's only accountancy firm since 2012. Colleagues describe him as modest and cautious with money, which makes the change all the more striking. Speculation has been rife.

The most obvious explanation is that he must have won a large sum of money. A lottery syndicate operating from the local pub has confirmed that he was not a member, however, so he can't have won there. Others suggest that he might have inherited a fortune from a distant relative, although a family friend says he has no known relatives. Presumably he was paid handsomely for some private consultancy, and for all we know, it could have been a bonus, although the firm's director insists that no such payments were made last year.

A third theory is more worrying. Some residents believe that he must have been taking funds from clients' accounts over a long period. If so, the sudden spending seems to have followed years of careful concealment. The firm has denied any irregularity, and the police say they have received no complaint, so the allegation may well be unfounded. A neighbour, who asked not to be named, claims to have seen him carrying boxes of documents late at night; he may have been shredding evidence, or he could simply have been tidying his office.

One explanation can be ruled out. Mr Vaughn can't have sold his house, since it is still registered in his name, according to local records.

For now, the accountant is away and cannot be reached for comment. Until he returns, the town will have to live with the mystery. As one resident put it, "Whatever the truth is, someone knows more than they are saying."

reading.title: The Quiet Millionaire
reading.intro: Read this opinion piece about an invented case and answer the questions.
paragraphs: When Walter Brandt died last spring at the age of eighty-one, the residents of Alder Street were astonished to learn that the quiet retired caretaker in number 14 had left more than three million dollars to the city's public library. By all accounts, Brandt had lived modestly. He wore the same grey coat for two decades, ate his lunch from a flask on a bench by the canal and, as one neighbour put it, "counted pennies as if they were gold coins". How, people wondered, had he come by such a fortune?

The speculation began almost immediately. Some argued that he must have inherited the money from a wealthy relative, though no such relative has been found. Others, pointing to his habit of reading the financial pages every morning, suggested that he might have been investing shrewdly for decades. A few, more romantic, insisted that he could have won a lottery and kept it secret, but lottery winners are rarely so disciplined, and the dates did not fit. One local paper even speculated that he may have been a retired spy, an idea that made for a good headline and very little else.

The truth, pieced together by his solicitor, was less dramatic but more instructive. Brandt had started saving at nineteen, when his first wage packet taught him that security was a form of freedom. He had never taken out a loan, never bought a new car and never, as far as anyone can tell, been tempted by an impulse purchase. Every month he had put aside a third of his income in a low-cost index fund and then, crucially, left it alone. Compound interest had done the rest. Anyone looking at the statements today can see that most of the fortune is simply growth on growth: the reward for patience.

Yet the story did not end there, and it is here that opinion divides. Several former colleagues recalled that Brandt had turned down invitations to dinners, weddings and even a retirement party, apparently to avoid chipping in for gifts. His one nephew, who lives abroad, insists that he can't have been happy: "A man who never spent a penny on himself must have been afraid of something." Others disagree. Someone who volunteered at the library three afternoons a week, remembered every borrower's name and left behind a note describing the reading room as "the best place I ever worked" can hardly have been unhappy. He may simply have valued different things.

The case raises uncomfortable questions about how we judge other people's money. We tend to assume that spending signals enjoyment and thrift signals deprivation, yet the link is far from automatic. A person who buys little may be practising a clear-eyed form of ethical consumption, refusing to fund waste, while a person who splashes out on every new gadget may be anxious or lonely. Equally, we should be wary of turning Brandt into a saint. Had he shared a little more of his wealth while alive, he could have eased the burden of neighbours who were living hand to mouth, and some of them feel, understandably, that his generosity came too late.

The library, for its part, has announced that the bequest will fund a new children's wing, to be named after him. Whether he would have approved of the plaque is another matter. He strikes me as the kind of man who would have considered it an unnecessary expense, and who might well have asked us to spend the money on books instead.

listening.title: Why did Rafa cancel?
listening.intro: Listen to three friends talking about a mutual friend. You can play it again.

lines.text: Did you see the group chat? Rafa's cancelled our weekend trip again, and he's the one who suggested it.
He must have run into money trouble. He hasn't been himself since March.
I don't think so. He can't have been short of cash. He bought a brand new motorbike last month.
Fair point. Then again, he might have taken out a loan for it. People do that all the time.
True. Or he could have been overspending on his credit card without realising. Remember how he picked up the bill for everyone at that sushi place?
Yeah, he must have spent a fortune that night. Honestly, he should have let us go Dutch.
He needn't have insisted, you're right. But I think he hates being seen as stingy.
Hmm. Do you think we should say something, or would that be prying?
I'd say it's a toss-up. If I were him, I'd rather someone asked than let me struggle in silence.
Agreed. Though we don't know for certain it's about money. He may just have been exhausted.
Right. He was working late all week, so he must have been running on empty.
Fine, let's invite him for coffee, my treat. No lecture about budgets, just a chat.
Perfect. And if it is money, at least he'll know he isn't alone.
I'll text him now. Fingers crossed.

items.prompt: What do the friends know for certain about why Rafa cancelled?
options: He told them he was ill
items.explain: It's all speculation.

items.prompt: Why does Eli think Rafa isn't short of cash?
items.explain: 'He bought a brand new motorbike last month'.

items.prompt: Eli thinks Rafa was right to pay for everyone at the sushi place.
items.explain: Eli says they should have let each person pay their own share.

items.prompt: Eli says it's a toss-___ whether they should ask him.
answers: up
items.explain: 'It's a toss-up' = está parejo.

items.prompt: What do they decide to do?
items.explain: Eli lo invita a un café.

tasks.prompt: Speculate: a friend who was always short of money suddenly buys a new car. What do you think happened?
questions: How do you think he paid for it?
Could there be an innocent explanation?
What would you say to him?
tasks.model: He might have received an inheritance, or he could have taken out a loan. Honestly, he can't have saved that much from his salary. He may also have been working extra hours, because he looked exhausted lately. For all we know, someone helped him, so I wouldn't jump to conclusions.
checklist: Use might/could/may have + past participle
Use can't have to rule something out
Include must have with evidence
Close with For all we know / jump to conclusions

tasks.prompt: Debate: Is it ethical to buy cheap fast fashion?
questions: Is it ever acceptable to buy fast fashion?
Who should be held accountable: shoppers or companies?
What is the role of greenwashing?
What would you change in your own habits?
tasks.model: On the one hand, many people can't afford ethical brands. On the other, it could be argued that cheap clothes exploit workers and the planet. Companies should be held accountable, yet shoppers needn't have bought so much in the first place. Personally, I try to buy less and buy better.
checklist: On the one hand… on the other…
It could be argued that…
Vocabulary: exploit, accountable, greenwashing
Clear personal position

tasks.prompt: Tell about a money mistake (yours or someone else's) and what you would have done differently.
questions: Have you ever spent money you regretted?
What should you have done instead?
tasks.model: Last year I splashed out on a gadget I barely used. I should have compared prices, and I shouldn't have bought it on impulse. I could have saved that money for a trip. It was a drop in the ocean for my budget, but the lesson stayed with me.
checklist: should have / shouldn't have + past participle
could have for a missed opportunity
At least one money idiom
Close with a lesson learned

repeat: He must have spent a fortune on that watch.
She can't have known about the debt.
They might have lost it on the train.
You should have read the small print.
You needn't have paid the whole bill.
For all we know, he gave it all away.
